name: Adam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We milk a hundred and sixty cows with two robot milkers I put in five years ago, so the cows milk themselves when they feel like it. My day starts at six with the laptop, checking which cows haven't visited the robot and whose milk looks off. Then it's the sugar beet and wheat, or fixing whatever broke overnight. My son Erik farms with me, plus two staff, and my wife Karin keeps us all fed and honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving problems. Every season there's a new one, and I enjoy figuring it out, whether it's a sick cow or a software update. What wears me out is the milk price. You can run the best farm in the county and still get paid whatever the dairy decides that month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: good tools, not magic. I'd say it at church and at the farmers' discussion group, where half the men think I'm mad for having robots already. I'd also say a good farmer uses every tool he can, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge from being early, and nothing much changes. That's fine. I'm fifty-eight and I don't need the world turned upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for herd records, feed planning and the beet spraying schedule, every day like now. I'd try new tools now and then and drop the useless ones. Savings stay at around four months of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would a plateau disappoint you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I like new things, but I'm also not stupid, most new things are rubbish. I'd rather have a plateau than a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be focused on instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Handing over to Erik properly. He's thirty-one and he's ready, he just needs me to step back, which Karin says I'm bad at.

S0.say: He'd say at church and his farmers' discussion group that AI turned out to be good tools rather than magic, and that a good farmer uses every tool he can.
S0.think: Privately it means he keeps his edge from adopting early and nothing much changes, which suits him at fifty-eight.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for herd records, feed planning and spraying schedules, trying new tools and dropping useless ones. Keeps savings at about four months and focuses on handing over to his son.
S0.quote: I'd rather have a plateau than a crash.
S0.fieldNote: Adam combines a strong appetite for technology with traditional faith and family values. He's confident and self-aware, admitting he's bad at stepping back. Succession to his son is the thread through his life, whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for farmers who are willing to work and learn. The market will reward the ones who adapt. I'd also say government should keep out of the way and let farms get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I'm already halfway there with the milkers, and Erik's sharp with software. My only worry is neighbours who won't change, and I'd feel bad for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot feed pusher and an automatic slurry scraper in the first year, about fifty thousand on a loan I could pay back in four years. I'd expand the herd by maybe thirty cows. And I'd get Erik to take on more of the planning with the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. It's my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring in next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feed pusher. It goes round the barn pushing feed back towards the cows every hour, day and night. That means more milk and less work for us at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your two staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep them both, but I'd train them to look after the machines. Lars, the older one, would grumble, but he's good with his hands and he'd learn. I'd rather pay for training than lose a good worker.

S1.say: He'd say this is a chance for farmers willing to work and learn, the market will reward those who adapt, and government should stay out of the way.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do well, already halfway there with robot milkers and a son who's sharp with software, though he'd feel bad for neighbours who won't change.
S1.do: Buys a robot feed pusher and slurry scraper in the first year for about fifty thousand on a four-year loan, and grows the herd by about thirty cows. Hands more AI-based planning to his son and trains his two staff on the machines.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, his kind of change.
S1.quote: That means more milk and less work for us at three in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: He moves first and sees steady change as a reward for effort, which matches his free-market outlook. He still protects his staff through training rather than cutting them. His confidence is backed by real experience with robots already on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should trust in God and in hard work and not panic. Farmers have survived worse. I'd say the government shouldn't rush in with rules that make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big dairy companies would go fully robotic and the milk price would drop. My head start would shrink, because everyone could buy what I have. I'd be fine for a while, but the loan on the milkers would feel heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to finish automating the farm within a year, so I'm as cheap as the big ones. I'd save harder too, aiming for six months of costs instead of four. And I'd sit down with Erik and decide whether the farm is his future or whether he should keep a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd still feel in control, but I'd not be relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're already automated. Does that make you safe with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than most, yes. But not safe. When everyone has robots, the advantage goes to whoever has the cheapest money, and that's not a family farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn how the robots work inside, not just how to use them. If farming goes, a man who can fix robots will always have work. And I'd tell him the farm is still his, whatever happens.

S2.say: He'd tell people to trust in God and hard work and not panic, because farmers have survived worse, and warn the government against rushing in with rules.
S2.think: Privately he expects big dairies to go fully robotic and milk prices to fall, shrinking his head start and making the loan on his milkers feel heavier.
S2.do: Pushes to finish automating the farm within a year to match big producers' costs. Saves harder toward six months of costs and urges his son to learn robot repair as a second skill.
S2.feel: Uneasy, still in control but not relaxed.
S2.quote: When everyone has robots, the advantage goes to whoever has the cheapest money, and that's not a family farm.
S2.fieldNote: Even this confident adopter sees the fast scenario eroding his advantage. His response is to move faster and build a cushion rather than ask for help. His advice to his son is practical and protective, rooted in family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare properly, so farmers should get on with it. I'd tell the discussion group to look at the robots now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years suits me. I'd finish automating, pay the milker loan off, and Erik would be in charge by the time it arrives. It's a challenge, but a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate in steps, the feed pusher this year, the scraper next year, paying as I go. I'd help Erik take over the business side, with me stepping back to two or three days a week by sixty-two. And I'd keep putting some profit into the farm rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it without borrowing too much. In two years I'm racing the big firms. In five I'm just running my farm well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd stop investing and just ride it out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around sixty-two, when Erik's fully in charge. Then it's his call, and I'd keep my nose out, or try to.

S3.say: He'd tell his discussion group there's time to prepare properly and that farmers should look at robots now rather than in year four.
S3.think: Privately five years suits him: he'd finish automating, pay off the milker loan and have his son in charge by the time AGI arrives.
S3.do: Automates in steps, paying as he goes. Hands the business side to his son and steps back to two or three days a week by sixty-two, putting profit back into the farm.
S3.quote: In two years I'm racing the big firms. In five I'm just running my farm well.
S3.fieldNote: With five years his anxiety from the fast scenario disappears. He sees the time as enough to fund change without heavy debt. His plan is as much about stepping back for his son as about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for families who are willing to work. I'd encourage young people to learn practical skills and not wait for anyone to hand them a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be retired by then, watching Erik run a robot farm. That's not frightening to me, it's what I've been building towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep investing steadily, a machine every couple of years. I'd hand the farm to Erik around sixty-three, a bit earlier than I'd planned. And I'd keep some savings aside for Karin and me, maybe for a small place near our daughter Sigrid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to sixty-eight. Where are you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting at the kitchen table with Karin, watching Erik's robots through the window, and telling him what he's doing wrong. He'd ignore me, rightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time with the grandchildren. With ten years, there's no excuse not to.

S4.say: He'd encourage young people that ten years is plenty for families willing to work, and urge them to learn practical skills rather than wait for anyone to hand them a living.
S4.think: Privately he expects to be retired, watching his son run a robot farm, which he sees as what he's been building towards rather than something frightening.
S4.do: Keeps investing in a machine every couple of years and hands the farm to his son around sixty-three, earlier than planned. Saves for a small place near his daughter for himself and his wife.
S4.quote: Sitting at the kitchen table with Karin, watching Erik's robots through the window, and telling him what he's doing wrong.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, AGI feels like the completion of his life's project. His traditional values show in his focus on family and grandchildren. He remains the most comfortable with change of any situation he describes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the big money moves fastest. What would help is fair access to cheap credit for family farms, so we can buy machines at the same price as the big companies. Not grants, just a level field.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether farming families will still mean anything. I think they will, if we keep teaching our kids to work. The robots will do the milking, but the family still has to decide what the farm is for.

headlineQuote: The robots will do the milking, but the family still has to decide what the farm is for.
portrait: Adam Larsen, 58, runs a dairy farm with robot milkers, sugar beet and wheat alongside his son Erik and two staff. He's a confident early adopter who uses AI every day, combined with traditional faith, family values and a belief in free markets. He's calm in most scenarios and only uneasy if AGI arrives in two years and shrinks his head start. With five or ten years, he sees AGI as the natural completion of his plans to automate and hand the farm to his son.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because big money moves fastest and his early-adopter advantage would shrink.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to cheap credit for family farms so they can buy machines at the same price as big companies.
